say: This six-hundred-sixty-tonne steel ball hangs near the top of Taipei one-oh-one. And it's there on purpose.
Tall towers sway in strong wind, like a ruler flicked on a desk, and people on the top floors feel seasick.
So engineers hung the ball on cables between floors eighty-seven and ninety-two, swinging at the tower's own rhythm.
When wind pushes the tower one way, the ball lags behind and pulls it back.
Eight hydraulic pistons turn that motion into heat, cutting the sway by up to forty percent.
In twenty fifteen, Typhoon Soudelor hit Taipei, and the ball swung a full metre, its biggest move on record.
The ball took the hit, so the people inside barely felt it.
Follow for the hidden engineering all around you.
